name: RAD-140
lead: RAD-140, whose International Nonproprietary Name is vosilasarm and which is also called RAD140, EP0062 and by the black-market name Testolone, is an orally taken, nonsteroidal selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM). It was developed by Radius Health in 2010, first described in the literature in 2011, and is now under development by Ellipses Pharma for androgen receptor-positive, estrogen receptor-negative, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer.[1] Earlier plans to develop it for sarcopenia, osteoporosis and cancer cachexia were discontinued.[1]

No human data on its effect on lean body mass have been published as of 2022 according to Wikipedia; the only completed human trial was a small first-in-human phase 1 study in postmenopausal women with breast cancer.[1][2] Animal studies in rats and monkeys showed muscle-stimulating effects with weaker effects on the prostate, which is the basis of its tissue-selective label.[1]

RAD-140 is sold online for physique and performance purposes and is on the World Anti-Doping Agency's prohibited list.[1][3] Published case reports describe drug-induced liver injury, myocarditis and heart failure in people who used it non-medically, and Wikipedia notes that many products sold online as a specific SARM contain none of it or unrelated substances.[1][4][5][6][7][8]
infobox: Not approved for any medical use; WADA prohibited

paras: Vosilasarm is not approved for any medical use. Development for hormone-sensitive breast cancer is ongoing, and a phase 1/2 study proposal published in 2023 planned to recruit up to 128 patients.[1]

Wikipedia states the compound is sold by black-market Internet suppliers for physique and performance enhancement, often at doses that have not been evaluated in clinical trials, and that social media has played an important role in spreading non-medical SARM use.[1] On T Nation, posters mention it as a fat-loss or muscle option, as something a gym partner takes between cycles with MK-677, in connection with a bodybuilder's reported use, or during recovery attempts after a testosterone cycle.[9][10][11][12]

The first-in-human trial (NCT03088527) was a phase 1 study in 20 postmenopausal women with hormone receptor-positive breast cancer, started in October 2017 and completed in 2020; Wikipedia describes oral doses of 50 to 150 mg per day with a maximum tolerated dose of 100 mg per day, and results published in 2019, 2020 and 2022.[13][1] Reported side effects in women with metastatic breast cancer included vomiting, dehydration, decreased appetite and weight loss, lowered SHBG in all participants, raised PSA in most, and abnormal liver tests including elevated AST (59 percent) and ALT (46 percent).[1]

No clinical trial has tested RAD-140 for muscle building or appearance in healthy people, and the doses reported in non-medical use (5 to 30 mg per day, according to Wikipedia) overlap with but are not the same as the cancer trial doses, with unknown effects.[1] A cell-based and in silico study compared RAD-140 with two other SARMs for androgen receptor activity.[14]

Animal findings include a 2011 preclinical report in rats and monkeys, and a 2023 study in which 10 weeks of RAD140 in female mice negatively affected skeletal muscle adaptation, frailty status and mortality risk.[1][15] In cynomolgus monkeys, vosilasarm cut testosterone by about half and altered lipids.[1]

Liver injury is the most documented harm from non-medical use. Case reports include a 24-year-old man with cholestatic liver injury confirmed on biopsy after five weeks of use, a 29-year-old with jaundice after about three months, and a 52-year-old man who used two supplements containing RAD-140 or RAD-140 with LGD-4033.[4][8][16] A further report and literature review covers SARM-induced liver injury more broadly.[17]

Cardiac cases have also been reported: a 16-year-old boy with myopericarditis after a first dose, a young man with acute myocarditis, and a case described as heart failure from SARM abuse.[5][6][7] The authors of the myopericarditis report note that the drugs' side effects, which can be life-threatening, are not well characterized.[5]

A forum poster described suppressed testosterone and cholesterol after a cycle of two SARMs at doses lower than lifters recommended, and others report erectile and libido problems after use.[18][12] Wikipedia says masculinisation and long-term effects are unknown.[1]

RAD-140 binds the androgen receptor with a Ki of about 7 nM (versus 10 nM for DHT) and good selectivity over other steroid receptors.[1] In castrated rats it stimulated levator ani muscle at a dose far below that needed to affect prostate weight, a roughly 33-fold difference, and in young monkeys it dose-dependently increased body weight and numerically increased lean mass.[1] Agonist effects in androgen receptor-expressing breast cancer cell lines underlie its investigation in breast cancer.[1]
Oral bioavailability was 27 to 63 percent in rats and 65 to 75 percent in monkeys; the human elimination half-life is reported as 45 to 60 hours.[1]
Vosilasarm is an oxadiazole aniline derivative; other aniline SARMs include AC-262536 and ACP-105.[1]

Radius Health developed RAD140 in 2010, and the 2011 paper describing its design and preclinical characterisation said phase 1 studies for cancer cachexia were being prepared, but these were not completed or published. The compound was repurposed for breast cancer.[1] The first-in-human study ran from 2017 to 2020 and a phase 1/2 study was proposed in 2023.[1][13]

SARMs were added to the WADA Prohibited List in 2008, and analytical papers describe detection methods, including equine metabolite studies, forensic follow-up of adverse findings and a nanoparticle sensor for RAD-140 and other SARMs in serum.[3][19][20][21]

subs.h: Use in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities
paras: On T Nation, posters ask whether others have tried RAD-140, mention using it with MK-677 between cycles, report one RAD-140 cycle in a year of SARM cycling, or ask about sourcing it; one poster said an article about a competitor's use made him want to take it.[9][10][11][22] A Wikipedia-sourced warning that product content may differ from labelling applies to these purchases.[1]

timeline.event: First described in the literature, with plans for cachexia trials that were not completed.[1]
First-in-human phase 1 study in postmenopausal women with breast cancer begins.[13]
Phase 1 study completed; case reports of liver injury linked to RAD-140 supplements appear.[1][16]
Case reports of RAD-140 liver injury and acute myocarditis published.[4][6]
Phase 1/2 breast cancer study proposal published.[1]
Case reports of myopericarditis and heart failure after RAD-140 use.[5][7]

lore.intro: RAD-140 is discussed on forums as a potent SARM, often described alongside other compounds in recovery and cycling contexts.[10][11][18]

claims.claim: RAD-140 builds muscle and burns fat with few side effects
claims.believers: A poster who read an article about a competitor's reported use said it made him want to take it, citing muscle mass, stamina and fat loss.[10]
claims.experts: No human trial has measured lean mass or fat change with RAD-140; animal studies show muscle stimulation and Wikipedia notes liver and hormonal effects in cancer trials.[1]

claims.claim: RAD-140 is safe for liver and heart at the doses people use
claims.believers: Users discuss it as a lower-risk alternative to steroids.[11]
claims.experts: Case reports document cholestatic liver injury, myocarditis and heart failure in users; authors say safety is poorly characterised.[4][5][6][7][8]

claims.claim: RAD-140 suppresses less testosterone than steroids
claims.believers: One poster said he ran a low-dose SARM cycle expecting mild effects but reported significant testosterone and cholesterol suppression.[18]
claims.experts: Monkey data show testosterone suppression of about half, and cancer trials report SHBG decreases.[1]

claims.claim: RAD-140 helps with recovery or restoring libido after a cycle
claims.believers: A poster who had erectile problems after a cycle said he used it followed by testosterone to recover.[12]
claims.experts: No studies tested RAD-140 for this purpose.[1]

claims.claim: Online RAD-140 products contain what they claim
claims.believers: Buyers often assume a labelled product is genuine.[22]
claims.experts: Wikipedia says many products sold online as SARMs contain none or unrelated substances; one case involved supplements that combined RAD-140 with LGD-4033.[1][16]
